   234	amount of CPU and memory it can provide for Pods. The scheduler ensures that,
   235	for each resource type, the sum of the resource requests of the scheduled
   236	containers is less than the capacity of the node.
   237	Note that although actual memory
   238	or CPU resource usage on nodes is very low, the scheduler still refuses to place
   239	a Pod on a node if the capacity check fails. This protects against a resource
   240	shortage on a node when resource usage later increases, for example, during a
   241	daily peak in request rate.
   242	
   243	## How Kubernetes applies resource requests and limits {#how-pods-with-resource-limits-are-run}
   244	
   245	When the kubelet starts a container as part of a Pod, the kubelet passes that container's
   246	requests and limits for memory and CPU to the container runtime.
   247	
   248	On Linux, the container runtime typically configures
   249	kernel {{< glossary_tooltip text="cgroups" term_id="cgroup" >}} that apply and enforce the
   250	limits you defined.
   251	
   252	- The CPU limit defines a hard ceiling on how much CPU time the container can use.
   253	  During each scheduling interval (time slice), the Linux kernel checks to see if this
   254	  limit is exceeded; if so, the kernel waits before allowing that cgroup to resume execution.
   255	- The CPU request typically defines a weighting. If several different containers (cgroups)
   256	  want to run on a contended system, workloads with larger CPU requests are allocated more
   257	  CPU time than workloads with small requests.
   258	- The memory request is mainly used during (Kubernetes) Pod scheduling. On a node that uses
   259	  cgroups v2, the container runtime might use the memory request as a hint to set
   260	  `memory.min` and `memory.low`.
   261	- The memory limit defines a memory limit for that cgroup. If the container tries to
   262	  allocate more memory than this limit, the Linux kernel out-of-memory subsystem activates
   263	  and, typically, intervenes by stopping one of the processes in the container that tried
   264	  to allocate memory. If that process is the container's PID 1, and the container is marked
   265	  as restartable, Kubernetes restarts the container.
   266	- The memory limit for the Pod or container can also apply to pages in memory backed
   267	  volumes, such as an `emptyDir`. The kubelet tracks `tmpfs` emptyDir volumes as container
   268	  memory use, rather than as local ephemeral storage.　When using memory backed `emptyDir`,
   269	  be sure to check the notes [below](#memory-backed-emptydir).
   270	
   271	If a container exceeds its memory request and the node that it runs on becomes short of
   272	memory overall, it is likely that the Pod the container belongs to will be
   273	{{< glossary_tooltip text="evicted" term_id="eviction" >}}.

    74	Figure 1. HorizontalPodAutoscaler controls the scale of a Deployment and its ReplicaSet
    75	
    76	Kubernetes implements horizontal pod autoscaling as a control loop that runs intermittently
    77	(it is not a continuous process). The interval is set by the
    78	`--horizontal-pod-autoscaler-sync-period` parameter to the
    79	[`kube-controller-manager`](/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/kube-controller-manager/)
    80	(and the default interval is 15 seconds).
    81	
    82	Once during each period, the controller manager queries the resource utilization against the
    83	metrics specified in each HorizontalPodAutoscaler definition. The controller manager
    84	finds the target resource defined by the `scaleTargetRef`,
    85	then selects the pods based on the target resource's `.spec.selector` labels,
    86	and obtains the metrics from either the resource metrics API (for per-pod resource metrics),
    87	or the custom metrics API (for all other metrics).
    88	
    89	- For per-pod resource metrics (like CPU), the controller fetches the metrics
    90	  from the resource metrics API for each Pod targeted by the HorizontalPodAutoscaler.
    91	  Then, if a target utilization value is set, the controller calculates the utilization
    92	  value as a percentage of the equivalent
    93	  [resource request](/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers/#requests-and-limits)
    94	  on the containers in each Pod. If a target raw value is set, the raw metric values are used directly.
    95	  The controller then takes the mean of the utilization or the raw value (depending on the type
    96	  of target specified) across all targeted Pods, and produces a ratio used to scale
    97	  the number of desired replicas.
    98	
    99	  Please note that if some of the Pod's containers do not have the relevant resource request set,
   100	  CPU utilization for the Pod will not be defined and the autoscaler will
   101	  not take any action for that metric. See the [algorithm details](#algorithm-details) section below
   102	  for more information about how the autoscaling algorithm works.
   103	
   104	- For per-pod custom metrics, the controller functions similarly to per-pod resource metrics,
   130	
   131	From the most basic perspective, the HorizontalPodAutoscaler controller
   132	operates on the ratio between desired metric value and current metric
   133	value:
   134	
   135	```math
   136	\begin{equation*}
   137	desiredReplicas = ceil\left\lceil currentReplicas \times \frac{currentMetricValue}{desiredMetricValue} \right\rceil
   138	\end{equation*}
   139	```
   140	
   141	For example, if the current metric value is `200m`, and the desired value
   142	is `100m`, the number of replicas will be doubled, since
   143	\\( { 200.0 \div 100.0 } = 2.0 \\).  
   144	If the current value is instead `50m`, you'll halve the number of
   145	replicas, since \\( { 50.0 \div 100.0 } = 0.5 \\). The control plane skips any scaling
   146	action if the ratio is sufficiently close to 1.0 (within a globally-configurable
   147	tolerance, 0.1 by default).
   148	
   149	When a `targetAverageValue` or `targetAverageUtilization` is specified,
   150	the `currentMetricValue` is computed by taking the average of the given
   151	metric across all Pods in the HorizontalPodAutoscaler's scale target.
   152	
   153	Before checking the tolerance and deciding on the final values, the control
   154	plane also considers whether any metrics are missing, and how many Pods
   155	are [`Ready`](/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/#pod-conditions).
   156	All Pods with a deletion timestamp set (objects with a deletion timestamp are
   157	in the process of being shut down / removed) are ignored, and all failed Pods
   158	are discarded.
   159	
   160	If a particular Pod is missing metrics, it is set aside for later; Pods
   161	with missing metrics will be used to adjust the final scaling amount.
   162	
   163	When scaling on CPU, if any pod has yet to become ready (it's still
   164	initializing, or possibly is unhealthy) _or_ the most recent metric point for
   165	the pod was before it became ready, that pod is set aside as well.
   166	
   167	Due to technical constraints, the HorizontalPodAutoscaler controller
   168	cannot exactly determine the first time a pod becomes ready when
   169	determining whether to set aside certain CPU metrics. Instead, it
   170	considers a Pod "not yet ready" if it's unready and transitioned to
   171	ready within a short, configurable window of time since it started.
   172	This value is configured with the `--horizontal-pod-autoscaler-initial-readiness-delay`
   173	flag, and its default is 30 seconds.
   174	Once a pod has become ready, it considers any transition to
   175	ready to be the first if it occurred within a longer, configurable time
   176	since it started. This value is configured with the
   177	`--horizontal-pod-autoscaler-cpu-initialization-period` flag, and its
   178	default is 5 minutes.
   179	
   180	The \\( currentMetricValue \over desiredMetricValue \\) base scale ratio is then
   181	calculated, using the remaining pods not set aside or discarded from above.
   182	
   183	If there were any missing metrics, the control plane recomputes the average more
   184	conservatively, assuming those pods were consuming 100% of the desired
   185	value in case of a scale down, and 0% in case of a scale up. This dampens
   186	the magnitude of any potential scale.
   187	
   188	Furthermore, if any not-yet-ready pods were present, and the workload would have
   189	scaled up without factoring in missing metrics or not-yet-ready pods,
   190	the controller conservatively assumes that the not-yet-ready pods are consuming 0%
   191	of the desired metric, further dampening the magnitude of a scale up.
   192	
   193	After factoring in the not-yet-ready pods and missing metrics, the
   194	controller recalculates the usage ratio. If the new ratio reverses the scale
   195	direction, or is within the tolerance, the controller doesn't take any scaling
   196	action. In other cases, the new ratio is used to decide any change to the
   197	number of Pods.
   198	
   199	Note that the _original_ value for the average utilization is reported
   200	back via the HorizontalPodAutoscaler status, without factoring in the
   201	not-yet-ready pods or missing metrics, even when the new usage ratio is
   202	used.
   203	
   204	If multiple metrics are specified in a HorizontalPodAutoscaler, this
   205	calculation is done for each metric, and then the largest of the desired
   206	replica counts is chosen. If any of these metrics cannot be converted
   207	into a desired replica count (e.g. due to an error fetching the metrics
   208	from the metrics APIs) and a scale down is suggested by the metrics which
   209	can be fetched, scaling is skipped. This means that the HPA is still capable
   210	of scaling up if one or more metrics give a `desiredReplicas` greater than
   211	the current value.
   212	
   213	Finally, right before HPA scales the target, the scale recommendation is recorded. The
   214	controller considers all recommendations within a configurable window choosing the
   215	highest recommendation from within that window. This value can be configured using the
   216	`--horizontal-pod-autoscaler-downscale-stabilization` flag, which defaults to 5 minutes.
   217	This means that scaledowns will occur gradually, smoothing out the impact of rapidly
   218	fluctuating metric values.

    45	## Prerequisites
    46	
    47	Network policies are implemented by the [network plugin](/docs/concepts/extend-kubernetes/compute-storage-net/network-plugins/).
    48	To use network policies, you must be using a networking solution which supports NetworkPolicy.
    49	Creating a NetworkPolicy resource without a controller that implements it will have no effect.
    50	
    51	## The two sorts of pod isolation
    52	
    53	There are two sorts of isolation for a pod: isolation for egress, and isolation for ingress.
    54	They concern what connections may be established. "Isolation" here is not absolute, rather it
    55	means "some restrictions apply". The alternative, "non-isolated for $direction", means that no
    56	restrictions apply in the stated direction. The two sorts of isolation (or not) are declared
    57	independently, and are both relevant for a connection from one pod to another.
    58	
    59	By default, a pod is non-isolated for egress; all outbound connections are allowed.
    60	A pod is isolated for egress if there is any NetworkPolicy that both selects the pod and has
    61	"Egress" in its `policyTypes`; we say that such a policy applies to the pod for egress.
    62	When a pod is isolated for egress, the only allowed connections from the pod are those allowed by
    63	the `egress` list of some NetworkPolicy that applies to the pod for egress. Reply traffic for those
    64	allowed connections will also be implicitly allowed.
    65	The effects of those `egress` lists combine additively.
    66	
    67	By default, a pod is non-isolated for ingress; all inbound connections are allowed.
    68	A pod is isolated for ingress if there is any NetworkPolicy that both selects the pod and
    69	has "Ingress" in its `policyTypes`; we say that such a policy applies to the pod for ingress.
    70	When a pod is isolated for ingress, the only allowed connections into the pod are those from
    71	the pod's node and those allowed by the `ingress` list of some NetworkPolicy that applies to
    72	the pod for ingress. Reply traffic for those allowed connections will also be implicitly allowed.
    73	The effects of those `ingress` lists combine additively.
    74	
    75	Network policies do not conflict; they are additive. If any policy or policies apply to a given
    76	pod for a given direction, the connections allowed in that direction from that pod is the union of
    77	what the applicable policies allow. Thus, order of evaluation does not affect the policy result.
    78	
    79	For a connection from a source pod to a destination pod to be allowed, both the egress policy on
    80	the source pod and the ingress policy on the destination pod need to allow the connection. If
    81	either side does not allow the connection, it will not happen.

**Decision memo — revise before production approval**

The proposed settings do not establish five-replica availability or safe completion of long requests. Approval should depend on coordinated rollout, scheduling, shutdown, security, and storage settings, followed by application and cluster testing. References below are local paths within the supplied `docs/` corpus.

1. **PDB protection differs across the three cases.** Node failure is involuntary: a PDB cannot prevent it, although unavailable Pods count against the budget. During an eviction-based node drain, `minAvailable: 5` permits one disruption from six healthy replicas; further evictions can block until replacements recover. This requires tools that honor the Eviction API. A Deployment rolling update is not constrained by the PDB, although its unavailable Pods consume the budget. Consequently, `maxUnavailable: 2` permits a rollout floor of four. Recommend `maxUnavailable: 0`, `maxSurge: 1`, with capacity for the surge; `maxUnavailable: 1` also aligns with a five-replica rollout floor. Neither configuration protects against concurrent failures.

   Sources: `docs/concepts/workloads/pods/disruptions.md:99–136`; `docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment.md:1189–1211`.

2. **Spread by zone, with an explicit outage tradeoff.** Configure a matching Pod selector, `topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone`, and `maxSkew: 1`; validate node labels. The topology key groups equally labeled nodes into domains. Under `DoNotSchedule`, skew limits the target domain’s matching-Pod count relative to the global minimum; violating placements remain pending. Under `ScheduleAnyway`, reducing skew is a preference, allowing placement despite imbalance.

   Prefer hard spreading if balanced placement outweighs replacement capacity during zone loss; choose soft spreading if scheduling into surviving zones takes priority. Unavailable-zone behavior depends on eligible domains, affinity, taints, and remaining nodes. With hard spreading and `minDomains: 3`, fewer than three eligible domains makes the global minimum zero, potentially blocking replacements. Omitting it defaults to one. Six evenly placed replicas imply two per zone, so losing one immediately leaves four. Spread constraints also do not guarantee balance after removals.

   Sources: `docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/topology-spread-constraints.md:82–130,527–529,605–623`.

3. **Separate startup, traffic eligibility, and restart decisions.** Use a startup probe whose `failureThreshold × periodSeconds` covers measured worst-case initialization. Other probes remain disabled until startup succeeds; their initial-delay clocks then begin. Use readiness to report whether the API can serve requests, including required database availability where appropriate. Failed readiness removes the Pod from matching Service endpoints without restarting its container. Use liveness for conditions where restarting helps, such as deadlock; avoid treating a temporary database outage as proof the API process needs restarting. Consecutive startup or liveness failures reaching the threshold trigger container restart behavior. Probe endpoints and timings are application choices requiring validation.

   Sources: `docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes.md:311–347,398–422`; `docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle.md:479–497,524–528`.

4. **Thirty seconds is a shutdown budget, not a completion guarantee.** The grace-period countdown begins before `preStop`, so the hook consumes that budget. The kubelet runs the hook before requesting TERM delivery to container processes. An overrunning hook can receive a small, one-off two-second extension; remaining processes are forcibly killed with `SIGKILL` when shutdown expires.

   Endpoint processing happens concurrently with local shutdown. Terminating endpoints remain temporarily in EndpointSlices, marked terminating with `ready: false`, excluding them from regular traffic; `serving` supports draining-aware consumers. These mechanisms do not establish that every long request completes. Implement application draining and signal handling, then size grace time for hook execution, outstanding requests, and cleanup.

   Sources: `docs/reference/kubernetes-api/workload-resources/pod-v1.md:1006–1008`; `docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle.md:581–639`.

5. **Resource requests and limits serve different purposes.** CPU requests inform scheduling and typically determine CPU weighting under contention; they are not a usage ceiling. Containers can exceed requests when resources are available. CPU limits impose throttling, potentially lengthening requests. Memory limits are enforced reactively through OOM handling and can terminate processes; they are not CPU-style throttling.

   Set measured CPU requests for all relevant containers because utilization-based HPA divides usage by requests. Missing relevant requests leave Pod CPU utilization undefined, preventing action for that metric. Inspect admitted Pods: when a limit exists without a request or admission default, Kubernetes copies the limit into the request.

   Sources: `docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers.md:18–53,63–66,252–265`; `docs/tasks/run-application/horizontal-pod-autoscale.md:89–102`.

6. **HPA deliberately moderates the raw ratio.** The basic calculation is the rounded-up current replica count multiplied by current/desired metric value. However, terminating and failed Pods are excluded; missing metrics and certain not-yet-ready CPU samples are set aside. Missing metrics are conservatively assumed at 100% of target for downscaling and 0% for upscaling. Not-yet-ready Pods further dampen an otherwise indicated scale-up through a 0% assumption.

   If recalculation reverses direction or falls within tolerance, scaling stops. Default tolerance is 0.1; readiness-related defaults include a 30-second initial-readiness delay and five-minute CPU initialization period. Downscale stabilization defaults to five minutes, selecting the highest recommendation within that window. Therefore observed utilization, HPA status, and actual scaling can differ. Resource metrics availability is a prerequisite.

   Sources: `docs/tasks/run-application/horizontal-pod-autoscale.md:113–118,130–218`.

7. **Replace default allow with explicit communication paths.** Establish namespace-wide ingress and egress isolation, then allow approved callers to the API port, API egress to database destinations and ports, matching database ingress, and necessary DNS queries. Identify actual resolver destinations and required ports in this cluster.

   Ingress and egress isolation are independent. Policies are additive unions: an overly broad allow remains effective despite another restrictive policy. For Pod-to-Pod connections, source egress and destination ingress must both permit traffic; replies to allowed connections are implicitly allowed. Enforcement requires a supporting network plugin/CNI: creating policy objects alone can have no effect. Test allowed and denied paths before promotion.

   Sources: `docs/concepts/services-networking/network-policies.md:45–81,105–122`; `docs/concepts/security/multi-tenancy.md:215–220`.

8. **Base64 is insufficient protection for Git-held Secrets.** The documentation describes base64 values as obscured, not secret; encoding satisfies the API representation requirement. Remove usable credentials from Git and select a protected delivery mechanism. Kubernetes Secrets are stored unencrypted in etcd by default, so enable encryption at rest and least-privilege RBAC, restricting access to necessary containers.

   Restrict workload creation permissions as well as direct Secret reads: someone authorized to create Pods in a namespace can read its Secrets through those Pods, including indirectly through Deployment creation. Encryption at rest does not resolve repository exposure or authorized API access.

   Sources: `docs/concepts/configuration/secret.md:35–48,306,453–457`.

9. **Treat PV reclamation and StatefulSet PVC retention separately.** Dynamically provisioned PVs inherit the StorageClass reclaim policy, defaulting to `Delete`. Changing the class is not a retroactive migration of existing PV policies; inspect and explicitly patch existing PVs. With `Retain`, deleting a PVC leaves a released PV containing previous data and requiring manual reclamation. With supported `Delete` behavior, reclamation removes both the PV and backing storage asset.

   StatefulSet deletion or scaling normally retains template PVCs. Its optional retention policy independently controls `whenDeleted` and `whenScaled`; `Delete` removes affected PVCs after Pods disappear, then PV reclamation determines storage disposal. The supplied documentation specifies the feature-gate prerequisite. Dynamic provisioning alone establishes no database durability or recovery guarantee.

   Sources: `docs/concepts/storage/persistent-volumes.md:178–210`; `docs/concepts/storage/storage-classes.md:126–135`; `docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/statefulset.md:387–423`.

10. **Prioritize rollout and validation as follows.**

   - **Before deployment:** remove exposed credentials, verify encryption and authorization, inspect actual PV reclaim and PVC retention policies, and test network isolation.
   - **Before enabling automatic changes:** measure startup and shutdown, configure probes and grace time, establish requests and limits, and verify resource metrics.
   - **Before production rollout:** validate zone labels and outage scheduling, reserve surge capacity, apply compatible rollout settings, and set an HPA minimum consistent with the intended six-replica baseline.
   - **Exercise failure paths:** test drains, failed rollouts, zone loss, missing metrics, database unavailability, long-request termination, and storage recovery.

   At least four limits remain empirical: request completion during shutdown, CPU utilization’s relationship to API latency, surviving-zone capacity, and database recovery/durability. The documents explain controls without establishing these outcomes. Topology-constrained storage also needs driver validation; supported `WaitForFirstConsumer` provisioning can account for Pod scheduling constraints.

   Sources: `docs/reference/kubernetes-api/workload-resources/horizontal-pod-autoscaler-v2.md:86–99`; `docs/concepts/storage/storage-classes.md:171–199`; validation follows the documented boundaries cited in answers 1–9.
